uChat.title: Chat assistant
uChat.body:
Ask and answer in a web page or app; the least access, the safest, and the most common use.

📍 Location: Using agents › Work alongside it › Chat assistant
⚙️ Usage layer: no model parameters change, only how you use it
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Talks, writes, explains, suggests.
  • Often has a few tools: web search, running a small piece of code, reading files you upload.
  • Some remember your preferences across chats (“memory”), which you can usually view and delete.

▶ How to use it

  • Treat it as a capable colleague who makes mistakes: check important numbers, sources and conclusions.
  • One topic per chat; when a chat gets very long, start a new one and paste in the key points.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

It does not touch your computer or accounts; the worst case is a wrong answer, which makes it the best place to start.

✅ Why this works

No setup: open it and use it.

⚠️ Limits / notes: It cannot see your project or files unless you paste them in; in a long chat, early content may fall out of the context window.

uIde.title: Coding agent in the editor
uIde.body:
Lives in your code editor: reads your project, edits files, runs commands, while you review and accept each change.

📍 Location: Using agents › Work alongside it › Coding agent in the editor
⚙️ Usage layer: no model parameters change, only how you use it
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Completion: as you type, it guesses the next lines.
  • Chat: select code and ask “what does this do?” or “change it to…”.
  • Agent mode: give it a task; it finds files, edits several places, runs tests, then shows you the changes (a diff).

▶ How to use it

  • Read each diff before accepting; roll back to an earlier checkpoint if needed (many tools save them automatically).
  • Keep a project rules file: code style, how to run tests, which folders not to touch; it is read in every time.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The risk in code changes is “what changed”; having every change pass your eyes as a diff is the simplest safeguard.

✅ Why this works

It does the legwork, you make the calls; works best in projects with tests.

⚠️ Limits / notes: It only knows what is in its context: in a large project it may start before reading the key file.

uCli.title: Command-line coding agent
uCli.body:
A coding agent in the terminal: reads and writes files, runs commands, uses git; a permission level decides how much it does on its own.

📍 Location: Using agents › Work alongside it › Command-line coding agent
⚙️ Usage layer: no model parameters change, only how you use it
🧪 Try it:

🎯 Role

  • Much like the editor agent, but easier to use on remote servers, in scripts and pipelines.
  • Three common levels: ask every step → allow edits, ask before commands → fully automatic.

▶ How to use it

  • Use the first two levels day to day; turn on “fully automatic” only in isolation (a container, a VM, a throwaway machine).
  • Allow-list commands: e.g. tests run freely, but delete, push and network access ask first.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The command line can do almost anything (delete files, change settings, send requests), so permissions are the core design of these tools.

✅ Why this works

Levels let you grant access by trust: the more familiar the job, the more you let go.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Fully automatic on your real computer: one wrong command can cause damage you cannot undo.

uCua.title: Browser / computer-use agent
uCua.body:
Operates web pages or a computer like a person: looks at screenshots / the page structure, then clicks, types, scrolls.

📍 Location: Using agents › Work alongside it › Browser / computer-use agent
⚙️ Usage layer: no model parameters change, only how you use it

🎯 Role

  • Each round: take a screenshot (or read the page’s accessibility tree) → the model decides where to click or what to type → the program does it → screenshot again.
  • Used on systems that have no API and can only be operated through the screen.

▶ How to use it

  • Run it in an isolated browser or VM; avoid logging in to important accounts.
  • Payments, sending and deleting must stop and wait for your confirmation.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

Screens are made for people and change often; letting the model look before each step is the general fallback when there is no API.

✅ Why this works

It can operate almost any website or program.

⚠️ Limits / notes: Slow and error-prone; text on a page may hide a prompt injection that steers it to do something else.
